classification_signals: The Summary mentions 'close observation of real case-studies' and 'Science and Technology Studies (STS) is adopted' (page 4). Chapter 4 details the methodology, including 'collection of “verbatim accounts of real-life interviews along with genuine documents”' and 'close reading' (page 70). It also describes 'in-field observations' (page 69) and the use of qualitative analysis software (Atlas.ti) for coding (page 73). Chapter 7 describes a focus group for evaluation (page 182).

limitations: Investigation of unpublished studies makes it impossible to build an initial literature-based overview of possible case-studies.
Research is a slow process due to the need to pass through many different gate-keepers that filter access to information.
The time-span required for a research study (e.g., PhD) may be incompatible with the often suspended nature of specific controversies.
In the Utrecht case study, it was not possible to get in touch with all practitioners (acoustic consultant, architects, developers) to build a satisfactory and non-partial view.
Issues of scale of representation emerged, as matters of concern had a much shorter duration in the second case study, making a common scale of representation potentially suboptimal.
The static nature of the maps, although divided in different zooms, was indicated as a complication in understanding, suggesting a need for more interactive visualizations.
minimum_safe_summary: This doctoral dissertation investigates the complex interplay of architecture, noise mitigation policies, and stakeholder interactions in urban transformations, adopting a Science and Technology Studies (STS) and Actor-Network Theory (ANT) perspective. Through detailed case studies in Turin, Italy, and Utrecht, Netherlands, the research reveals how noise mitigation goals are often influenced by a 'thick mesh' of human and non-human actors, leading to controversies and modifications in building design and policy implementation. Key findings highlight that performance-based policies, when accompanied by flexible guidelines, can effectively enroll architects as mediators in design processes, while overly prescriptive policies may hinder creative solutions and disconnect from living quality goals. The study also develops and evaluates novel visual vocabularies (maps) to represent these complex processes, demonstrating their efficacy in enhancing stakeholder awareness and interaction, though acknowledging the need for more interactive digital tools. Limitations include the challenges of accessing unpublished data and navigating gatekeepers in real-world case studies, as well as the time-consuming nature of such qualitative research.
